summary:
I developed an interactive, story-driven web platform featuring two animated guides—Soma (for The Moon Hub) and Mangal (for The Mars Hub)—that transform dense historical NASA mission logs into an engaging museum-style experience for school-age learners and space enthusiasts. Rather than presenting static lists of technical specifications, our website brings dormant robotic landers, descent stages, rovers, and scientific instruments to life through conversational mission logs, interactive timelines, landing site maps, and memorable "Did You Know?" facts. This addresses the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge by bridging the gap between complex archival space data and youth-friendly storytelling, inspiring the next generation to appreciate how past off-world hardware paved the way for modern space exploration.

details:
What Exactly Does It Do & How Does It Work?

The platform is structured into dedicated celestial hubs (Home, Moon, and Mars) designed to feel like exploring an off-world museum:

  • Character-Led Navigation: Users are greeted by Soma on the lunar surface and Mangal on the Martian surface. Clicking "SAY HI" initiates a guided narrative tour explaining why these environments preserve human hardware (such as the Moon's lack of wind, rain, or atmosphere keeping spacecraft frozen in time).
    • The Ranger Program (1961–1965): Chronicles NASA/JPL's "Kamikaze Photographers" (Rangers 1 through 9), detailing early failures (Ranger 4's computer timer failure) alongside breakthroughs (Rangers 7, 8, and 9 transmitting thousands of close-up television images before impact to help scout Apollo landing sites).
      1. Lunar Module Descent Stages: The six octagon-shaped launchpads (Eagle, Intrepid, Antares, Falcon, Orion, Challenger) wrapped in gold-colored Kapton thermal foil.
      2. Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles (LRVs): The three electric four-wheel-drive off-roaders deployed on Apollos 15, 16, and 17, detailing their distances driven (up to 35.9 km on Apollo 17) and scientific discoveries like orange volcanic glass beads.
      3. Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Packages (ALSEP): Nuclear-powered (SNAP-27 RTG) science stations that monitored moonquakes, heat flow, and solar wind until 1977, alongside the Laser Ranging Retroreflectors that remain active today—proving the Moon drifts away from Earth by ~3.8 cm per year.
      4. Human Artifacts: Engaging trivia cards such as "There are currently 6 pairs of tongs on the Moon."
  • The Mars Hub Archives: Guided by Mangal, visitors explore robotic hardware left on the Red Planet since 1976 across two main categories: Stationary Mars Landers and Mobile and Airborne Explorers. It covers early pioneers including Viking 1 (1975–1982, Chryse Planitia), Viking 2 (1975–1980, Utopia Planitia), and Mars Pathfinder (airbag landing system and base station relay for the Sojourner rover).

What Benefits Does It Have & What Do You Hope to Achieve?

  • Makes Space History Accessible to Youth: Translates dense archival NASA telemetry and engineering histories into bite-sized, visually engaging narratives tailored for school-age space enthusiasts.
  • Connects Engineering to Scientific Discovery: Explicitly links how a piece of hardware worked (e.g., SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generators surviving freezing lunar nights, or silver-zinc batteries powering mesh-wheeled rovers) to what humanity learned from it (e.g., discovering the Moon has a distinct crust, mantle, and core).
  • Preserves Off-World Heritage: Fosters awareness of historic lunar and Martian landing sites as humanity's first off-world archaeological monuments.
